title_en: Fragments on the First Letter to the Thessalonians
author: Severianus of Gabala
occasion: The surviving catena fragments explain passages from 1 Thessalonians, especially Paul's consolation of persecuted Thessalonian Christians and his teaching on the resurrection and the Lord's coming.
argument: Severianus explains that Paul wrote to comfort Thessalonian believers who were suffering persecution from their Greek neighbors and grieving the loss of relatives. He reports Paul's claim that the gospel came not only in word but also in power and wonders, and that Paul's boldness in preaching was not diminished by his sufferings at Philippi. On the resurrection, he argues that some righteous people will still be alive at Christ's coming, but the dead in Christ will rise first and the righteous will meet the Lord. He interprets the day of the Lord as Christ's sudden, unexpected coming, like a thief in the night, and explains that the night setting shows how the day exposes the evil deeds done at night. He also urges believers to remain watchful and to test prophetic utterances rather than despise or uncritically accept them.

outline.move: The prologue explains the Thessalonians' persecutions, Paul's consolation, his thanksgiving, and the roles of faith, love, and hope, with the triad treated twice in slightly varied wording.
Severianus comments on Paul's wording about afflictions and on the resurrection passage, arguing that some righteous people will still be alive at Christ's coming.
He supports the view that some will be taken alive at the coming by citing Gospel passages about Noah's days, the bridegroom at midnight, and the two in the bed and at the mill.

He interprets the day of the Lord as sudden, explains sleeping and waking as dying and living, and comments on quenching the Spirit, testing prophecies, and the preservation of spirit, soul, and body.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle and author of 1 Thessalonians, whose words Severianus explains.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: The Lord whose coming, resurrection of the dead, and saving death are central to the passage.

cast.name: Thessalonian Christians

voices.speaker: Paul

voices.speaker: Christ

voices.speaker: The bride, identified with the soul adorned with virtues

key_terms.sense: The coming or arrival of Christ at the end, the day of the Lord.
The resurrection of the dead in Christ at his coming.
Believers who have died, described as having fallen asleep.
The righteous who remain alive until the Lord's coming.
The day of the Lord, identified with Christ's coming, sudden and revealing.
The gift of the Spirit given to believers, distinct from soul and body.
The human soul, part of human nature together with the body.
The human body, part of human nature together with the soul.
Prophetic utterances or revelations in the church, which must be tested.
The spiritual gift given to believers, identified with the spirit.
The gospel message preached by Paul, accompanied by power and wonders.
The affliction or persecution suffered by believers.

scripture: The author cites 1 Thessalonians by standard New Testament book name and chapter/verse. Gospel citations are introduced generally as 'the Gospel' or 'the Gospels.' The bride's words in u01-rem-mid and u01-rem-close are from Song of Songs 5:2, but Severianus does not name the book; the identification is editorial. Psalm numbering is not relevant in these fragments.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is unknown.
The original addressee of the commentary is not stated in the fragments.
The precise extent and original structure of the commentary cannot be reconstructed from the catena fragments.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He interprets the day of the Lord as Christ's sudden, unexpected coming, like a thief in the night, and explains that the night setting shows how the day exposes the evil deeds done at night.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐν νυκτὶ δέ, ὅτι ἡ ἡμέρα ἐπιστᾶσα τὰ ἐν νυκτὶ φαῦλα ἀπελέγχει
_unresolved_facts.fix: He interprets the day of the Lord as Christ's sudden, unexpected coming, like a thief in the night. The night setting is mentioned, but the explanation given is that the day exposes the evil deeds done at night (τὰ ἐν νυκτὶ φαῦλα ἀπελέγχει), not specifically that 'the day exposes the evil deeds done at night' as a theological point about judgment—though this is close to the source, the brief's phrasing slightly overstates the explanatory connection.
The source uses "Θεσσαλονικέων" (genitive plural) and "οἱ ἐν Θεσσαλονίκῃ Χριστιανοί", but not the nominative form "Θεσσαλονικεῖς" as claimed in source_forms.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The bride, identified with the soul adorned with virtues: sections ["u01-rem-mid", "u01-rem-close"]
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἀλλ' ἡ νύμφη καὶ τῷ τῶν ἀρετῶν κόσμῳ κοσμουμένη ψυχὴ...ἐγὼ καθεύδω, καὶ ἡ καρδία μου γρηγορεῖ
_unresolved_facts.fix: The bride's voice appears in u01-rem-mid (the quotation from Song of Songs), but in u01-rem-close the bride is referred to in third person ("ταύτῃ τοι καὶ οὐ διέλαθεν αὐτὴν οὕτω καθεύδουσαν ἡ φωνὴ τοῦ νυμφίου"), not as a speaking voice. The brief should note that the bride is a referenced figure in u01-rem-close, not a speaking voice there.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὁ κύριος δηλοῖ ἐν τῷ Εὐαγγελίῳ λέγων
_unresolved_facts.fix: Christ's voice is also present in u01-rem-close through the Gospel citation about two in bed and at the mill (δύο ἔσονται ἐν κλίνῃ...), though this is embedded in the u01-rem-mid section's continuation. More importantly, the brief misses that Christ is cited as "ὁ σωτήρ" in u01-rem-mid, not just "ὁ κύριος" or Gospel formulae.
